subject: ophthalmology
title: Diabetic retinopathy, hypertensive retinopathy and vascular occlusions

steps.tx: Chronic hyperglycemia initiates **non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy**, characterized by microaneurysms, dot-and-blot hemorrhages, and lipid hard exudates resulting from breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier. As capillary non-perfusion spreads, ischemic retina develops cotton-wool spots representing axoplasmic flow stasis, venous beading, and intraretinal microvascular abnormalities. The 4-2-1 rule defines severe non-proliferative disease when diffuse intraretinal hemorrhages appear in four quadrants, venous beading in two quadrants, or microvascular shunts in one quadrant. This stage carries a fifty percent one-year risk of proliferative retinopathy, necessitating close retinal surveillance.
steps.say: Diabetic retinopathy begins with non proliferative changes driven by chronic hyperglycemia, capillary basement membrane thickening and pericyte loss. Microaneurysms appear as tiny red dots, while leaking capillaries produce intraretinal blot hemorrhages and lipid rich hard exudates. Progressive capillary closure leads to ischemic cotton wool spots, venous beading and irregular shunt vessels. When clinicians identify severe disease using the four two one rule, the eye faces a high risk of developing neovascularisation within twelve months. Strict control of blood glucose, blood pressure and lipids is essential.

steps.tx: The leading cause of visual impairment in diabetes is **diabetic macular oedema**, occurring at any retinopathy stage when fluid accumulates in the central retina. Optical coherence tomography quantifies central macular thickness and identifies cystoid edema or subretinal fluid. First-line management employs intravitreal injections of anti-vascular endothelial growth factor agents like aflibercept, ranibizumab or bevacizumab to reduce vascular permeability and restore acuity. Focal laser photocoagulation seals leaking microaneurysms, while sustained-release intravitreal dexamethasone implants serve pseudophakic or anti-VEGF refractory eyes, requiring monitoring for cataract progression and intraocular pressure elevation.
steps.say: Diabetic macular oedema is the most frequent cause of central visual loss in diabetic patients and can develop during any retinopathy stage. Breakdown of the endothelial blood retinal barrier allows fluid and proteins to leak into the macula, creating cystoid spaces that disrupt retinal architecture. Optical coherence tomography accurately measures macular thickening and guides therapeutic decisions. First line therapy relies on regular intravitreal injections of anti VEGF agents, which reduce vascular leakage and improve vision. Intravitreal steroid implants or focal laser provide valuable alternatives in refractory cases.

steps.tx: Retinal venous thrombosis produces sudden, painless unilateral vision loss in **central retinal vein occlusion**, typically caused by arteriosclerotic compression of the central vein by an adjacent thickened artery at the lamina cribrosa. Ophthalmoscopy reveals extensive flame and blot hemorrhages across all four quadrants, tortuous dilated veins, cotton-wool spots, and disc edema, known as a stormy sunset. Fluorescein angiography distinguishes non-ischemic from ischemic occlusion with extensive capillary non-perfusion. Ischemic occlusion carries a high risk of rubeosis iridis and neovascular glaucoma, termed ninety-day glaucoma, demanding panretinal photocoagulation.
steps.say: Central retinal vein occlusion causes sudden, painless unilateral visual blurring when a thrombus blocks the central retinal vein at the lamina cribrosa. Ophthalmoscopic examination demonstrates a dramatic stormy sunset appearance, characterized by widespread flame shaped hemorrhages in all four quadrants, engorged tortuous veins and optic disc swelling. Fluorescein angiography distinguishes non ischemic from ischemic disease, where extensive capillary non perfusion creates a severe risk of anterior segment neovascularization. Patients with ischemic occlusion must be monitored closely to detect rubeosis iridis and prevent ninety day neovascular glaucoma.

steps.tx: An ophthalmic emergency, acute **central retinal artery occlusion** causes sudden, catastrophic, painless blindness. Funduscopy reveals profound retinal opacification from intracellular edema, against which the thin fovea transmits underlying vascular choroid as a prominent cherry-red spot. Blood columns in attenuated arterioles break into segmented boxcarring. Urgent emergency interventions within ninety minutes attempt to dislodge the embolus through ocular massage, anterior chamber paracentesis, and intraocular pressure-lowering agents. Giant cell arteritis must be excluded urgently by measuring erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein to prevent fellow eye involvement.
steps.say: Central retinal artery occlusion is an ocular emergency presenting as sudden, profound, painless loss of vision. The inner retina suffers acute ischemic infarction, turning cloudy and milky white on funduscopic examination. Because the fovea is extremely thin, the underlying vascular choroid shines through as a vivid cherry red spot. Retinal arterioles appear markedly narrowed, with segmented boxcarring of red blood cells. Attempted emergency measures include digital ocular massage and paracentesis to dislodge the obstructing embolus. Giant cell arteritis must be ruled out immediately to prevent bilateral blindness.

steps.tx: A vital anatomical variation present in twenty percent of individuals is a **cilioretinal artery**, originating from the posterior ciliary circulation rather than the central retinal artery. When central retinal artery occlusion occurs, this patent vessel preserves perfusion to the papillomacular bundle, maintaining a central island of normal vision despite peripheral blindness. Branch retinal artery occlusion causes localized wedge-shaped retinal whitening corresponding to an embolic plaque, frequently a glistening cholesterol Hollenhorst plaque from carotid atheroma. Every retinal arterial occlusion demands cardiovascular investigation, including carotid Doppler ultrasonography and echocardiography.
steps.say: Presence of a patent cilioretinal artery can preserve central vision during central retinal artery occlusion because it derives blood from the posterior ciliary system rather than the central retinal artery. In affected patients, a small central island of macula remains perfused and pink, sparing reading vision despite extensive surrounding retinal infarction. In branch retinal artery occlusion, a discrete wedge of retina turns pale, often with a visible glistening cholesterol Hollenhorst plaque lodged at an arterial bifurcation. Every retinal arterial event mandates comprehensive cardiovascular evaluation to identify source emboli.
